description: Ascension Studios is an innovation-driven team passionate about exploring the intersection of artificial intelligence, software development, and scientific discovery. For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we have chosen “Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars” to address a critical challenge in humanity’s journey toward becoming an interplanetary civilization.
summary:
THEIA (Terrestrial Habitat Evaluation and Interplanetary Analogue) is a web app that finds the places on Earth that best resemble a chosen Moon or Mars base site. It measures all three worlds with one ruler: open NASA elevation and temperature data are cut into 132,098 terrain patches, each 118 km wide at the same 3.7 km pixel size, sampled without polar distortion, which matters for the lunar south pole. A self-supervised neural network ensemble, AnalogNet, learns a terrain “fingerprint” from these patches without any human labels.

For any target, such as Shackleton rim for Artemis or Jezero crater on Mars, THEIA ranks all 53,070 Earth land patches on four mission-relevant axes: terrain, rover mobility, thermal environment and bare ground. Every score comes with an uncertainty range and an explanation of why the site matches.

Known analog sites were held out from training and design, and THEIA rediscovers them far better than chance (p = 0.0005 for Mars). This turns analog site selection from expert intuition into a transparent, testable, planet-wide search, so field tests for astronauts, rovers and instruments can happen in the right places.
details:
THEIA answers a question every analog field campaign faces: for a given site on the Moon or Mars, which places on Earth are most alike, on the properties that matter for the mission, and how sure can we be? A researcher picks a target, such as Shackleton rim (an Artemis III candidate region), Jezero crater, or any point they click on the 3D Moon or Mars globe, and chooses a mission purpose. THEIA returns the ten best Earth analogs with scores, uncertainty ranges and explanations, shown on an interactive 3D globe.

How it works.

One ruler for three worlds: LRO LOLA (Moon), MGS MOLA (Mars) and NOAA ETOPO 2022 (Earth) elevation are resampled into 118 km patches of 32×32 pixels at exactly 3.7 km per pixel. Each patch is sampled on its own flat local grid, so the poles are not stretched. That gives 132,098 patches, spread evenly over each globe.

AnalogNet: a small convolutional neural network (about 0.18 million parameters) learns a 32-number terrain fingerprint through self-supervised contrastive learning (“spot the twin”). Two altered views of the same landscape must produce the same fingerprint. No human labels and no analog lists are used, and it trains on all three worlds together. Five networks with different seeds form an ensemble: their spread is the error bar and their agreement is a confidence vote.

Four-axis matching: terrain fingerprint, rover mobility (slope and roughness), thermal environment (LRO Diviner and the Mars Climate Database compared with MODIS land-surface temperature) and bare ground (MODIS vegetation index). Presets reweight the axes for rover testing, ice and resources, or landform science.

Explainability: feature-by-feature comparisons and occlusion saliency maps show which terrain drove each match. A one-click PDF report documents the result.

Validation. We ran a rediscovery test: 26 known Mars analog sites and 12 known Moon analog sites were never used for training or design. For Mars, their mean score is 86.1 against 69.8 for random land (p = 0.0005), and 65% of them fall in Earth’s top 10% (random: 19%). The Moon gives 84.3 against 69.9 (p = 0.005). The full model beats a non-neural baseline and every ablation, and its votes are well calibrated (calibration error 0.067). THEIA also proposes new candidate analogs for field checks, such as sites in Greenland, Baffin Island and the Altyn-Tagh and Kunlun mountains.

Benefits and impact. THEIA replaces one-site-at-a-time expert selection with a transparent, planet-wide and testable search. It helps NASA and its partners choose where to test astronauts, rovers and instruments, and it reveals overlooked analog sites. It is fully open data and runs in any browser.

Tools. Python, PyTorch, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, Streamlit, Plotly and Matplotlib; CesiumJS for the 3D globes. Data access through NASA PDS, NASA POWER, NASA Trek and Microsoft Planetary Computer (STAC). The app is deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud.

Creativity. As far as we know, this is the first shared AI terrain space for Earth, the Moon and Mars together. It pairs a striking holographic 3D globe with honest uncertainty, mission-specific matching and a published validation, rather than a single opaque similarity score.

Factors we considered. Equal scale and no polar distortion across worlds; the risk of the AI simply learning “which planet is this”; uncertainty and calibration; using only open, citable data; explainability for scientists; and stated limits. Those limits are: regional scale only (no boulders), no mineralogy layer yet, and Mars temperatures from a climate model. New candidates are hypotheses for field checks.
